sentences: Eleven men come toward us in a single line along a sandy riverbank, their bodies bent forward.
Each wears a strap across his chest, and every strap leads back to a heavy barge.
Only one young man in the middle holds his head up.
This is Barge Haulers on the Volga by the Russian painter Ilya Repin, who worked on it from 1870 to 1873.
It is oil on canvas and about 2.
8 metres wide.
It belongs to the State Russian Museum in St Petersburg.
In Russia these workers were called burlaki.
They walked along the bank and pulled boats upstream, against the current.
Repin first saw them on the Neva River as an art student, and later remembered being shocked that people were tied to boats in place of animals.
In the summer of 1870, Repin travelled to the Volga with the landscape painter Fyodor Vasilyev and others, and stayed in the village of Shiryaevo.
There he got to know the haulers and made many studies.
The figures in the painting are based on real men he met.
Look at the second man from the left, at the front.
He has a rag tied around his head.
His name was Kanin, and he had been a priest before he lost his position.
Repin was drawn to his broad forehead and deep eyes, and wrote that the man seemed like a saint.
Now find the young man in the centre of the line.
Everyone else leans forward, but he leans back and grips the strap on his chest.
His head is raised, as if he wants to break free.
His pink shirt is the one bright colour in a group of heavy browns and greys.
Look at the barge behind the men.
The flag on its mast hangs upside down.
Far away on the water, near the right edge, a small steamboat sends up smoke.
It was not in the first version and was added later, a quiet sign that machines could already do this work.
The horizon is low, so the men rise up large against the sky.
Follow the line of their heads as it goes up and down.
It feels like the rhythm of heavy steps that stop and start again.
When the finished painting was shown in 1873, the critic Vladimir Stasov praised it loudly, and Fyodor Dostoevsky admired that none of the men begs the viewer for pity.
Grand Duke Vladimir, a son of the tsar, bought it, and in 1918, after the revolution, it moved to the museum.
Step back and see the whole scene.
Under the wide river and sky, eleven men become one long line pulling a single boat.
Today, think of the people beside you who help you pull your own heavy load.
